teaching.task: # HMS Year 11 V17 (The body and mind in motion): classifying motor skills. How do you classify any movement skill, and why does the classification change how it should be practised? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: The syllabus gives four ways to classify a skill, and each one asks a different question. The first asks which muscles do the work. A gross skill uses large muscle groups for force and whole-body coordination, like running or a tackle. A fine skill uses small muscle groups for precision, like a dart throw or a golf putt. Most sport skills are both. Her shot uses her legs and trunk for force, and her fingertips to control the release. So ask which part limits it. When you tire, precision often drops faster than force. So a skill limited by its fine part should sometimes be practised tired, not only fresh. The second question is where the movement starts and ends. A continuous skill has no clear start or finish. The end of one cycle is the start of the next, like running or swimming. A discrete skill is one short unit with a clear start and end, like a penalty kick or a free throw. A serial skill is a chain of discrete parts in a fixed order, like a gymnastics routine or a triple jump. This scale decides whether a skill can be broken into parts for practice. Serial skills can. Continuous skills are mostly taught as a whole, because the rhythm is the skill. Kick and pull drills are practice parts, rejoined to the full stroke quickly. That answers the second puzzle. And with a serial skill, practise the joins too, because that's where it fails. A jumper who drills the hop, the step and the jump separately still has to arrive at each phase with the right speed. The third question changes practice the most: how predictable is the environment? A closed skill happens somewhere stable, like a golf putt or a shot put. Nobody interferes, and the goal is one consistent movement, so repeating it under the same conditions is right. An open skill happens somewhere that keeps changing, like passing in a match. Now the skill is reading the situation and choosing a movement, as well as doing it. That reading is called perceptual demand. Back to the shooter. An unguarded shot from one spot is closed. A match shot is open: a defender closing, the pass early, her feet not set. She's trained the doing half, and the reading half has had no practice at all. It's not nerves. It's the drill. But closed practice isn't useless. Earlier, you saw a beginner has no attention to spare, so she starts closed. The mistake is staying there. And a faster or harder closed drill is still closed. Open practice needs a decision made from information she can't know in advance.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus gives four ways to classify a skill, and each one asks a different question. The first asks which muscles do the work. A gross skill uses large muscle groups for force and whole-body coordination, like running or a tackle. A fine skill uses small muscle groups for precision, like a dart throw or a golf putt. Most sport skills are both. Her shot uses her legs and trunk for force, and her fingertips to control the release. So ask which part limits it. When you tire, precision often drops faster than force. So a skill limited by its fine part should sometimes be practised tired, not only fresh.

scenes.teachingReason: The second question is where the movement starts and ends. A continuous skill has no clear start or finish. The end of one cycle is the start of the next, like running or swimming. A discrete skill is one short unit with a clear start and end, like a penalty kick or a free throw. A serial skill is a chain of discrete parts in a fixed order, like a gymnastics routine or a triple jump. This scale decides whether a skill can be broken into parts for practice. Serial skills can. Continuous skills are mostly taught as a whole, because the rhythm is the skill. Kick and pull drills are practice parts, rejoined to the full stroke quickly. That answers the second puzzle. And with a serial skill, practise the joins too, because that's where it fails. A jumper who drills the hop, the step and the jump separately still has to arrive at each phase with the right speed.

scenes.teachingReason: The third question changes practice the most: how predictable is the environment? A closed skill happens somewhere stable, like a golf putt or a shot put. Nobody interferes, and the goal is one consistent movement, so repeating it under the same conditions is right. An open skill happens somewhere that keeps changing, like passing in a match. Now the skill is reading the situation and choosing a movement, as well as doing it. That reading is called perceptual demand. Back to the shooter. An unguarded shot from one spot is closed. A match shot is open: a defender closing, the pass early, her feet not set. She's trained the doing half, and the reading half has had no practice at all. It's not nerves. It's the drill. But closed practice isn't useless. Earlier, you saw a beginner has no attention to spare, so she starts closed. The mistake is staying there. And a faster or harder closed drill is still closed. Open practice needs a decision made from information she can't know in advance.

scenes.teachingReason: The fourth question is who decides when it starts. A self-paced skill starts when the performer chooses, like a free throw. An externally paced skill starts in response to something outside them, like returning a serve, or a sprint start on the gun. These usually line up with closed and open, but they're not the same thing. A sprint start is externally paced, because the gun sets the timing, but it's closed, because the lane never changes. So practise the movement over and over, and practise reacting to an unpredictable gun as a separate job. Pacing also shows where pressure falls. A self-paced skill gives time to prepare, so a routine helps, but nerves have time to build too. An externally paced skill gives no time, so practice trains anticipation against real, varied cues.

scenes.teachingReason: Each scale is a line, not two boxes, and the four are independent, so every skill gets four answers. The combination decides the practice.
